title: Interactive compression with logarithmic input-length overhead
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) such that every two-party protocol \(\pi\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, under every joint input distribution \(\mu\), has a simulation \(\rho\) with distributional error at most \(1/100\) and worst-case communication at most
\[
K\bigl(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1\bigr)\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil\quad\text{bits}?
\]
Here \(n\ge1\), the protocol and simulation model, internal information cost \(I_{\mu}\), and joint-transcript error are defined below. There is no restriction on the finite communication cost of \(\pi\), and \(K\) must be independent of \(n,\mu,\pi\).

This is an explicitly selected editorial version of the source's proposed logarithmic-loss question. The source's surrounding paragraph concerns two-party internal information, despite the article's multiparty title. It already reports that compression without an overhead is impossible. The particular logarithmic factor, constant error, additive regularization and worst-case transcript-simulation guarantee below are specified here rather than attributed verbatim to its informal sentence.

source_formulation.text: Put differently, is it always possible to compress the communication cost of a protocol to its information cost?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: The question asks how much communication is forced by interaction beyond the information actually transferred. A general small-overhead simulation would strengthen the connection between information-theoretic lower bounds and communication complexity, with consequences for direct-sum phenomena. A matching obstruction would show why correlated inputs prevent a near-information-cost account of interactive communication.
status_note: The 2016 source and its expanded version explicitly leave a small-loss two-party compression direction open while acknowledging the failure of no-loss compression. This card spells out a particular logarithmic-input-length, internal-information, joint-transcript simulation variant. Because the source does not uniquely select all of those conventions, the exact editorial combination is labeled uncertain rather than represented as a verbatim source conjecture. The dated later-result checks and explicit editorial scope decision are recorded in the individual audit; no exhaustive current-status certificate or Lean verification is claimed.

progress.text: A primary separation for relations shows an exponential gap between information and communication, with much larger input lengths; its parameterization matters for an input-length-dependent allowance.
The source distinguishes impossible no-loss two-party compression from a proposed small-loss question, mentioning a logarithmic dependence on input size.

The inspected Rao–Sinha revision simplifies a Boolean-function separation. Its input tables are sufficiently large that the low-information protocol itself uses only a constant times their logarithmic bit length.
Braverman–Kol establish compression with a different external-information benchmark and original-communication dependence.
A preprint gives many-copy amortized characterizations using zero-error information; these are not the stated simulation of every prescribed one-copy transcript.

category_assignment.reason: The main task is interactive protocol compression to information cost, without a differential-privacy requirement.

importance.reason: A central structural question connecting interactive information, compression and direct-sum lower bounds across communication complexity. The general correlated-input case captures a broad barrier, beyond one protocol family or a multiparty implementation detail. The selected logarithmic-loss regime is an explicit editorial specification of the substantial source question, and this importance judgment does not certify that exact variant as a verbatim later conjecture.

sentences: The underlying question concerns two-party interactive communication, even though its source article studies multiparty protocols.
A protocol can transmit many more bits than its internal information cost under the input distribution.
The proposed precise target allows a logarithmic factor in input bit length and a fixed total-variation error when both parties reconstruct the transcript.
Exact compression without loss is already known to fail, while results for external information or independent inputs address different targets.
A complete Lean answer must prove this explicitly specified universal simulation bound or a lower bound refuting every proposed universal constant.

definitions:
Alice has \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), Bob has \(y\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and the pair \((X,Y)\) has an arbitrary probability distribution \(\mu\) on this finite product. The inputs may be correlated. Both parties know \(n\), the description of \(\pi\) and \(\mu\). Neither party is initially given the other party's realized input. No promise is placed on the support of \(\mu\).

A protocol uses one finite string \(R\) of shared fair random bits and two finite strings \(R_A,R_B\) of private fair random bits. The three strings are mutually independent and independent of \((X,Y)\). Their finite lengths may depend on the protocol and are not charged as communication. A length of zero is allowed. For each fixed public string, the protocol is a finite rooted binary communication tree: every internal node designates Alice or Bob, and the selected player sends one bit determined by their own input, private string, public string and the earlier messages. That bit selects the next child. A leaf terminates communication. The owner of the next message and termination are therefore determined by the public string and common message history, rather than by an uncharged timing channel. The transcript of communicated bits is \(M\), and the augmented transcript is \(T=(R,M)\). Both parties observe every communicated bit. A protocol is defined on every input pair and every coin choice. Its worst-case communication \(\operatorname{CC}(\pi)\) is the maximum number of transmitted bits over all these executions; it is finite but may be arbitrarily large.

All local computation, protocol descriptions and shared randomness are free. There is no restriction on the number of rounds or the local running time, and no privacy requirement. No advice depending on the other party's realized private input or quantum resources are supplied; all initial resources are exactly those specified above. Protocols for different \(n,\mu,\pi\) may be unrelated. This is an existence statement about finite communication protocols, not an efficient compiler for producing one from a table of \(\mu\).

For a finite random variable \(U\), its base-two Shannon entropy is
\[
H(U)=-\sum_{u}\Pr[U=u]\log_2\Pr[U=u],
\]
where \(0\log_2 0=0\). Conditional entropy \(H(U\mid V)\) is the average of \(H(U\mid V=v)\) weighted by \(\Pr[V=v]\), with zero-probability terms omitted. The conditional mutual information is
\[
I(U;W\mid V)=H(U\mid V)-H(U\mid V,W).
\]
The internal information cost in bits is
\[
I_{\mu}(\pi)=I(X;T\mid Y)+I(Y;T\mid X).
\]
All variables use the joint law of \(\mu\) and the three independent coin strings of \(\pi\). Including \(R\) in \(T\) accounts for public randomness; private coins are not included in that transcript. This is internal information, not the external quantity \(I(X,Y;T)\), and not the distinct multiparty public-information measure introduced in the source. The quantity is finite, nonnegative and at most \(2n\).

A simulation \(\rho\) is another finite protocol in the same model, with its own independent shared and private fair coins. At its terminal leaf Alice outputs a value \(T_A\) determined by her local view and Bob outputs \(T_B\) determined by his. These values lie in the finite set of augmented transcripts possible for \(\pi\), together with a failure symbol \(\bot\). Output descriptions and their lengths are not communication costs. The simulated public string of \(\pi\) is part of these output values; it need not equal \(\rho\)'s actual public string.

Let \(P\) be the law of \((X,Y,T,T)\) produced by drawing \((X,Y)\sim\mu\) and executing \(\pi\). Let \(Q\) be the law of \((X,Y,T_A,T_B)\) produced by drawing the same input distribution and executing \(\rho\). Regard both as distributions on the same finite product space, assigning zero mass to impossible original outcomes and to original failures. The simulation error is their total variation distance
\[
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)=
\frac12\sum_{x,y,t_a,t_b}|P(x,y,t_a,t_b)-Q(x,y,t_a,t_b)|.
\]
Thus the requirement preserves correlation with the inputs and agreement between the parties' reconstructed transcripts, except for total variation at most \(1/100\). It is stronger than reproducing only an output bit of a particular function or only the unconditioned marginal law of \(T\). Error is averaged under \(\mu\) and the coins, whereas communication is worst case over every input pair and every coin string, including pairs of \(\mu\)-probability zero. There is no joint simulation of many independent copies. The \(+1\) in the cost bound avoids a zero-information boundary convention, and the logarithm is of the input bit length \(n\), not the number of possible inputs, the transcript length or the number of rounds.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal compression statement or its full negation. Equivalently, a positive answer gives one absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) and proves
\[
\forall n\ge1\ \forall\mu\ \forall\pi\ \exists\rho:\quad
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)\le\frac1{100}
\ \land\
\operatorname{CC}(\rho)\le
K(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
A negative answer must prove that for every proposed \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\), there are \(n,\mu,\pi\) in the stated domain for which every simulation with error at most \(1/100\) has communication strictly larger than that bound. A positive theorem only for product input distributions or public-coin original protocols does not cover the universal domain, although a matching lower bound within either subclass can refute the universal statement. Refuting only constant-overhead compression does not refute the logarithmic allowance. An expected-communication upper bound must be converted to the specified worst-case guarantee; error slack and an increased absolute constant can permit such a conversion. A theorem for external or multiparty public information must establish the claimed conclusion for the internal-information measure defined here to qualify. Likewise, failure of one simulation construction is not a lower bound for all simulations. The chosen constant simulation error is part of the mathematical proposition; the benchmark asks for a proof of that proposition or negation, rather than an approximate numerical verdict.

context_blocks.text: Interactive information measures what two participants learn about each other’s inputs during a conversation. The number of transmitted bits can be much larger. The source asks whether most of that discrepancy can always be removed while retaining the relevant behavior.

Reading the complete source paragraph changes the interpretation of the imported excerpt. It discusses the two-party question and says that compression with no loss is already ruled out. The open direction permits a small loss, giving logarithmic input-size dependence as an example.

The paper subsequently introduces a different public-information measure for multiparty computation and proves a compression theorem for it with logarithmic factors. That theorem cannot be substituted for a solution to the preceding two-party internal-information question.

Internal simulation reconstructs the original transcript for both participants while retaining its joint distribution with their inputs. The survey explicitly distinguishes this stronger requirement from merely computing the same total Boolean function. This card selects the transcript-simulation version.

Known exponential separations rule out compression solely to a fixed constant times information in general. Such statements must be compared with input size before treating them as a refutation of a logarithmic-input-length allowance.

Product-distribution compression assumes independent inputs. Compression to external information uses another information measure. These important positive results concern different domains or benchmarks from the present arbitrary-distribution internal target.

Internal I uses the augmented transcript including the public random string. All quantities are finite under finite-domain, bounded-communication, finite-coin conventions. Simulation compares the joint laws including both inputs and both outputs to the diagonal ideal transcript law, so matching only a marginal or a final Boolean answer does not qualify. Local work is free and protocols may depend nonuniformly on the known distribution; no effective construction from arbitrary real probabilities is required.

Rao–Sinha input-bit calculation: with their depth m and alphabet k, each party holds N=k^m+ceil(log2 k) sum_{r<m} k^r bits. Thus log2 N=Theta(m log k). Figure5.1, not the literal Theorem1.1 statement, shows at most m exchanges of two k-ary symbols plus final output bits, so the original low-information protocol communicates O(log N). A p3 triple-logarithm sentence conflicts with the corollary parameterization; do not repeat it as a verified bound. The explicit bit count and protocol itself suffice for the non-refutation check.

GKR2015 Section1.1.1 has quadruple-exponential inputs and triple-exponential low-information communication, while the shown lower bound is only exponential in k. Relations are within the universal transcript domain, but the actual length parameters mean this separation is not a demonstrated refutation of the selected logarithmic allowance.

Suruga arXiv2608.04141v1 defines prior-free IC0 of a relation and many-copy amortized expected/worst-case communication. Theorems1–2 do not promise one-shot simulation of a given protocol at its distribution-specific internal information cost. Only definitions and theorem scope were checked; no independent verification of its new proofs or a resolution of this card is asserted.
